content: Adolescent females, particularly those in younger age groups, frequently encounter barriers to accessing modern contraceptive methods. These barriers are influenced by geographical, political, and cultural factors. In 2015, the estimated birth rate in developing regions was 56 per 1,000, compared to 17 per 1,000 in developed regions. The objective of this study was to identify school-based interventions that effectively improved contraceptive use among adolescents. The research included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in middle schools or high schools, where the majority of participants were 19 years old or younger. The interventions focused on promoting one or more effective contraceptive methods, with primary outcomes being pregnancy rates and contraceptive use. The search for eligible trials was conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, CENTRAL, ERIC, Web of Science, POPLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, up until June 6, 2016. Titles and abstracts were screened, and data were extracted and verified by two authors. Methodological quality was assessed, and statistical analyses were performed using appropriate measures, such as Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and adjusted mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes. Meta-analysis was not conducted due to the heterogeneity of interventions and outcome measures. The review included 11 trials, comprising 10 cluster RCTs and one individually randomized trial. Sample sizes for the cluster RCTs ranged from 816 to 10,954 participants, with a median of 24 clusters. Most studies were conducted in the United States and the United Kingdom, with one trial each from Mexico and South Africa. The analysis focused on trials with moderate-quality evidence and measurable intervention effects. Three trials implemented interactive sessions aimed at preventing pregnancy and HIV/STIs. One trial involved a multifaceted two-year program. After the first year and 12 months following the second year, participants in the intervention group were more likely to report using effective contraception during their last sexual encounter (adjusted ORs 1.62 ± SE 0.22 and 1.76 ± SE 0.29), using condoms during their last sexual encounter (adjusted ORs 1.91 ± SE 0.27 and 1.68 ± SE 0.25), and engaging in less frequent unprotected sex in the past three months (ratios of adjusted means 0.50 ± SE 0.31 and 0.63 ± SE 0.23). Another trial compared two multifaceted two-year programs: one focused on sexual risk reduction and the other on risk avoidance (abstinence-focused), against usual health education. At three months, the risk reduction group was less likely to report not using a condom during their last sexual encounter (adjusted OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.96) and less likely to report unprotected sex in the past three months (adjusted OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.95). At three and 15 months, the risk avoidance group was also less likely to report not using a condom during their last sexual encounter (adjusted ORs 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.93; and 0.61, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.85). Additionally, the risk reduction group demonstrated higher scores for condom knowledge compared to the usual-education group. A third trial implemented a peer-led program consisting of eight interactive sessions. At 17 months, participants in the intervention group were less likely to report using oral contraceptives during their last sexual encounter compared to the teacher-led group (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.91). However, this difference may not have been statistically significant if adjustments for clustering had been made. At five and 17 months, the peer-led group showed a greater mean increase in knowledge about HIV and pregnancy prevention compared to the control group. An additional trial focused on knowledge outcomes. Participants who received a session on emergency contraception (EC) were more likely to correctly identify the time limits for using hormonal EC (pills) and non-hormonal IUDs as EC methods compared to those who did not receive the session. The authors concluded that most trials emphasized condom use as a means of preventing STIs, HIV, and pregnancy, although some studies addressed a broader range of contraceptive methods. The overall quality of evidence was low, primarily due to limited information on intervention fidelity, the analysis of subsamples rather than the full randomized population, and high rates of participant attrition.
